cases.title: Emergency department to step-down: hyperglycemic crisis in a young adult

patient.history: Type 1 diabetes since age 11 (insulin glargine 20 units nightly, insulin lispro with meals). No other conditions.

entries.text: Health history: Type 1 diabetes since age 11 (insulin glargine 20 units nightly, insulin lispro with meals). No other conditions. Last menstrual period 2 weeks ago.

1400: Vomiting since last night; unable to keep fluids down. Abdominal pain 6/10, diffuse. Drowsy but oriented x3; answers slowly. Respirations deep and rapid. Fruity odor to breath. Mucous membranes dry; skin warm. Capillary refill 3 seconds. Lungs clear bilaterally. Pupils equal and reactive. States she has skipped her glargine for 3 days because she could not afford the refill.

1440: 12-lead ECG: sinus tachycardia 122/min with flattened T waves and prominent U waves. Hand grips weak bilaterally. Insulin infusion bag prepared by pharmacy and at bedside; not yet started. First liter of lactated Ringer's infusing.

2000: Transferred to step-down at 1830. Alert, oriented, conversing in full sentences. Nausea resolved; sipping water. Insulin infusion running at 5.8 units/h since 1610. IV fluid: lactated Ringer's with KCl 20 mEq/L at 250 mL/h. Hourly point-of-care glucose: 1800 286, 1900 241, 2000 236 mg/dL.
0700: Ate half of breakfast tray without nausea. Insulin glargine 17 units subcut given at 0700 per transition order. Insulin infusion continues at 2.9 units/h with dextrose 5% in IV fluid.
1405: Lactated Ringer's 1,000 mL/h IV for 2 h, then reassess
1405: Regular insulin IV infusion 0.1 units/kg/h (5.8 units/h); no bolus

1405: Potassium per DKA protocol: K <3.5 mEq/L give KCl 10 mEq/h IV and do not start insulin until K is >3.5; K 3.5-5.0 add KCl 20-30 mEq to each liter of IV fluid; K >5.0 no potassium, recheck in 2 h
1405: Point-of-care glucose every 1 h; BMP, venous blood gas, and beta-hydroxybutyrate every 4 h; continuous cardiac monitoring
1405: When glucose is <250 mg/dL, add dextrose 5% to IV fluid and decrease insulin infusion to 0.05 units/kg/h (2.9 units/h); target glucose about 200 mg/dL until DKA resolves
Day 2 0630: Insulin glargine 17 units subcut at 0700; stop insulin infusion 2 h after glargine if DKA resolution criteria met

cases.title: Sickle cell pain crisis: comfort, complications, and opioid safety
cases.setting: Emergency department, then adult medical unit

patient.history: Sickle cell anemia (HbSS). Hydroxyurea daily. Home morphine extended-release 15 mg PO every 12 h and oxycodone 10 mg PO every 4 h as needed for pain crises. Individualized pain plan on file from hematology. Baseline hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL.

entries.text: Health history: Sickle cell anemia (HbSS). Hydroxyurea daily. Home morphine extended-release 15 mg PO every 12 h and oxycodone 10 mg PO every 4 h as needed for pain crises. Individualized pain plan on file from hematology. Baseline hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL.

0910 (arrived 0850, triaged 0855): Pain 9/10 in lower back and both thighs since last night, 'like my usual crises.' Took oxycodone 10 mg at 0300 and 0600 without relief. Grimacing and lying very still. Sclerae mildly icteric; client states 'my eyes are always like this.' Lungs clear; no cough. SpO2 94% on room air. Drinking water from his bottle; mucous membranes moist. Capillary refill less than 3 seconds.

Day 2, 1400: Hydromorphone PCA (demand doses only) since admission. Reports new right-sided chest pain, worse with deep breaths, and a dry cough since 1100. Has used the incentive spirometer twice since last evening. Crackles at right base. Awake and alert (POSS 1). Chest x-ray 1330: new right lower lobe infiltrate. Hematology notified; at bedside 1355.

Day 3, 1000: Red blood cells 10 mL/kg (700 mL) transfused day 2, 1700-2030, without reaction. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin continuing. Oxygen 2 L/min by nasal cannula. PCA continuous (basal) infusion added at 0200 for uncontrolled pain; home extended-release morphine was not held. 0950: drowsy, drifts off to sleep mid-conversation but easy to arouse (POSS 3). Pain 3/10.
0905: Analgesia per individualized SCD pain plan: IV hydromorphone now; reassess pain every 15-30 min and repeat per plan until pain controlled
0905: Oxygen if SpO2 <95% on room air; continuous pulse oximetry; sedation assessment (POSS) with every opioid reassessment
Admission: Hydromorphone PCA per plan; incentive spirometry while awake; ambulate as tolerated; local heat to painful areas as requested

Day 2, 1400: Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin PO (doses per pharmacy); oxygen to keep SpO2 above 95%; type and crossmatch; transfuse RBCs 10 mL/kg; notify hematology immediately if SpO2 <90% despite oxygen or respiratory distress increases

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1400 nurses' note. Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

tokens.text: Vomiting since last night; unable to keep fluids down.
States she has skipped her glargine for 3 days
because she could not afford the refill.

rationale.short: Missed basal insulin, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, ketotic breath, dehydration and drowsiness point to a hyperglycemic crisis with volume loss.

t8.text: Kussmaul respirations compensate for metabolic acidosis.

t20.text: No basal insulin: the usual trigger of DKA in type 1 diabetes.

t6.text: Orientation is preserved; drowsiness is the concern.

t16.text: Clear lungs argue against pneumonia as a trigger.

expanded.takeaway: Missed basal insulin + deep, rapid breathing + vomiting = suspect DKA; check ketones, pH and potassium first.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 per correct selection, -1 per incorrect selection; item score cannot go below 0.

items.stem: The 1410 laboratory results are available. For each finding, specify how it relates to the client's care at this time.

columns.label: Must be corrected before insulin is started
Abnormal, but expected to correct as glucose falls

rationale.short: Glucose, ketones, pH and bicarbonate meet DKA criteria (pH 7.0-7.25 and HCO3 10-<15 = moderate). K 3.2 must be corrected before insulin. Na 131 is dilutional from hyperglycemia.

r6.text: pH <7.3 is a diagnostic criterion; 7.14 = moderate.

r2.text: Insulin drives K into cells; consensus delays insulin until K >3.5 while giving K 10 mmol/h.

r4.text: Hyperglycemia pulls water into plasma; Na rises about 1.6 per 100 mg/dL glucose fall. No sodium replacement is needed.

expanded.takeaway: Check potassium before every DKA insulin start; a low K turns insulin into the most dangerous order.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: 1 point for each correct response; no deduction for incorrect responses.

references.locator: Table: DKA diagnostic criteria and severity; potassium replacement; sodium shift with glucose

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: Before insulin is started, the client is at highest risk for {{cause}}, as evidenced by the {{e1}} and the {{e2}}.

options.text: a life-threatening dysrhythmia from worsening hypokalemia
hypoglycemia from the planned insulin infusion
cerebral edema from rapid fluid resuscitation
fluid overload from crystalloid at 1,000 mL/h

rationale.short: K 3.2 with U waves and weak grips shows hypokalemia already affecting muscle and conduction; insulin will lower K further.

cause.text: Cerebral edema is rare in adults and nothing shows it now; glucose 486 makes hypoglycemia unlikely before insulin; clear lungs and BP 96/58 argue against overload.

e1.text: K 3.2 is below the 3.5 threshold. Glucose, sodium and creatinine reflect DKA and volume loss, not dysrhythmia risk.

e2.text: U waves = hypokalemic conduction change. Drowsiness and Kussmaul breathing reflect acidosis; clear lungs are normal.

expanded.takeaway: In DKA, total-body K is depleted even when serum K looks normal. A low serum K is an emergency once insulin starts.
expanded.pointsLost: Rationale scoring: cause must be correct to earn any points, then 1 point per correct linked effect (max 2).

references.locator: Potassium: if K <3.5 mmol/L, delay insulin and give K replacement

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1410 results, the 1440 note, and the ED orders. Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give regular insulin 0.1 units/kg IV push before the infusion
Give oral potassium chloride with sips of clear liquids
Start KCl 10 mEq/h IV on an infusion pump
Keep the insulin infusion on hold until potassium is above 3.5 mEq/L
Start the insulin infusion at 5.8 units/h now because glucose is 486 mg/dL
Request IV sodium bicarbonate for the pH of 7.14

rationale.short: Fluids and potassium first; insulin waits until K >3.5. Monitor rhythm and glucose closely.

o9.text: Isotonic fluid 500-1,000 mL/h for the first 2-4 h.

o2.text: Glucose every 1-2 h during IV insulin.

o7.text: Unsafe with K 3.2; glucose is not the priority.

o1.text: No bolus ordered; it would lower K further.

o8.text: Bicarbonate is not routine unless pH <7.0.

o3.text: She is vomiting; the protocol calls for IV K.

expanded.takeaway: Order of DKA care: fluids, then potassium check, then insulin.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 per correct selection, -1 per incorrect selection; item score cannot go below 0.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1900 results and the 2000 note. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

options.text: decrease the insulin infusion to 1.5 units/h
decrease the insulin infusion to 2.9 units/h
continue the insulin infusion at 5.8 units/h
stop IV fluids because she is drinking
change to 0.45% sodium chloride without dextrose
add dextrose 5% to the IV fluid
stop potassium because the level is normal
give KCl 40 mEq IV over 1 hour
add sodium bicarbonate to the IV fluid
continue KCl 20 mEq in each liter of IV fluid

rationale.short: Glucose 241 then 236 is <250 while pH 7.24, HCO3 14 and BHB 3.1 show ongoing ketoacidosis. Per order: add dextrose and halve insulin to 0.05 U/kg/h (2.9 units/h).

d1.text: Stopping insulin would let ketosis rebound; 5.8 risks hypoglycemia; 1.5 is not ordered.

d2.text: Stopping fluids is premature; D50 is for hypoglycemia; fluid without dextrose cannot carry ongoing insulin.

d3.text: K 4.1 is in the 3.5-5.0 band, so keep 20-30 mEq/L. Stopping risks hypokalemia; a 40 mEq bolus is not ordered; pH 7.24 does not need bicarbonate.

expanded.takeaway: Glucose falls faster than ketones clear. Keep insulin going and add dextrose until DKA has resolved.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: 1 point for each correct response; no deduction for incorrect responses.

client_needs.activityStatement: Titrate dosage of medication based on assessment and ordered parameters

references.locator: When glucose <250 mg/dL add 5-10% dextrose and reduce insulin to 0.05 U/kg/h; K 20-30 mmol/L when <5.0

items.stem: It is 0700 on hospital day 2. The nurse decides whether the insulin infusion can be stopped as ordered. For each finding, specify whether it is valid evidence that DKA has resolved.

columns.label: Not a valid basis for judging resolution

rationale.short: Resolution = ketones <0.6 mmol/L plus pH >=7.3 or HCO3 >=18. All are met, so with glargine given at 0700 the infusion can stop as ordered.

r6.text: Urine tests mainly acetoacetate, can stay positive after ketonemia clears, and the consensus says not to use it.

r2.text: Potassium is not a resolution criterion; it guides replacement, not when to stop insulin.

r3.text: Chloride is not a criterion; mild hyperchloremia is common in recovery.

expanded.takeaway: Judge DKA resolution by blood ketones and pH/bicarbonate, not urine ketones, potassium or chloride.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: 1 point for each correct response; no deduction for incorrect responses.

rationale.short: Severe pain unrelieved by home opioid and SpO2 below 95% need action now. Icterus, clear lungs, moist membranes and brisk refill are baseline or reassuring.

t2.text: Severe VOC pain: start analgesia within 30 min of triage.

t4.text: Home dose failed; recent opioid use guides the IV dose.

t12.text: Oxygen is indicated for SpO2 <95% on room air.

t8.text: Chronic hemolysis; client confirms it is baseline.

t10.text: No current sign of acute chest syndrome.

items.stem: For each finding at 0910, specify whether it is consistent with the client's chronic baseline or requires intervention now.

rows.text: Pain 9/10 after two home oxycodone doses

columns.label: Consistent with chronic sickle cell baseline

rationale.short: Compare with the client's own baseline. Chronic hemolysis explains the anemia, reticulocytosis, hyperbilirubinemia and icterus. Low SpO2 and uncontrolled pain need action.

r1.text: Within 1 g/dL of baseline 8.2; transfusion is not indicated for VOC alone.

r2.text: Close to the clinic value of 3.1.

expanded.takeaway: Abnormal is not the same as acute in SCD. Trend against the client's own baseline.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: On hospital day 2, the client is most likely developing {{cause}}, as evidenced by the {{e1}} and the {{e2}}.

options.text: PCA set to demand doses only

rationale.short: New infiltrate with fever, cough, pleuritic pain and hypoxemia during a VOC admission is acute chest syndrome.

cause.text: POSS 1 and RR 28 rule out opioid respiratory depression. A new infiltrate with fever fits ACS better than PE. Splinting does not cause fever or an infiltrate.

e1.text: Infiltrate is the defining finding. Pain 7/10 is nonspecific; POSS 1 shows the client is alert; admission Hgb was baseline.

e2.text: Fever and cough are lower respiratory signs. Demand-only PCA lowers sedation risk; bilirubin and creatinine are near baseline.

expanded.takeaway: Any new respiratory sign during VOC = evaluate for ACS with chest x-ray and SpO2.
expanded.pointsLost: Rationale scoring: cause must be correct to earn any points, then 1 point per correct linked effect (max 2).

items.stem: Which orders should the nurse anticipate for the client at 1400 on day 2? Select all that apply.

options.text: Discontinuation of the PCA to protect respiratory drive
Simple red blood cell transfusion of 10 mL/kg
Strict bed rest until the infiltrate clears
IV fluid at twice the maintenance rate
Oxygen titrated to keep SpO2 above 95%
IV cephalosporin plus an oral macrolide
Continued opioid analgesia with sedation and SpO2 monitoring

rationale.short: ACS: antibiotics, oxygen >95%, simple transfusion when Hgb is >1 g/dL below baseline (6.8 vs 8.2), and continued analgesia with monitoring.

o2.text: ACS rec 4: 10 mL/kg if Hgb >1 g/dL below baseline.

o8.text: Pain still 7/10; splinting worsens ACS; monitor sedation.

o1.text: Untreated pain worsens splinting; POSS 1 shows no oversedation.

o9.text: Avoid meperidine unless it is the only effective opioid.

o4.text: Reserved for rapid progression, e.g. SpO2 <90% despite oxygen.

o5.text: IV hydration no more than maintenance in euvolemic clients.

expanded.takeaway: Simple transfusion vs exchange depends on the trajectory. Know the escalation triggers.

rows.text: Give IV diphenhydramine with each PCA dose to prevent itching
Apply oxygen and titrate to keep SpO2 above 95%
Call hematology at once if SpO2 falls below 90% despite oxygen
Apply local heat to the painful thighs as requested
Withhold PCA doses until the cough resolves

rationale.short: Support oxygenation, lung expansion and comfort, keep analgesia going, and know the escalation trigger.

r2.text: If needed, antihistamines are given orally and not with each opioid dose.

r1.text: Strong recommendation; he used it only twice.

r5.text: Local heat and distraction are recommended adjuncts.

r6.text: Undertreated pain increases splinting; he is alert.

expanded.takeaway: Comfort measures (heat, spirometry, mobility) are active treatment in SCD, not extras.

rationale.short: ACS is responding, but a PCA basal rate added without holding the long-acting opioid has caused oversedation. POSS 3 with RR 10 needs immediate action.

r1.text: Objective sedation scale shows excessive sedation.

r2.text: Down from 28; with sedation this signals opioid-induced hypoventilation.

expanded.takeaway: Good SpO2 on oxygen can hide hypoventilation. Score sedation with every reassessment.

items.stem: A client taking an antidepressant reports feeling unwell. Complete the diagram: choose the condition the client is **most** likely experiencing, 2 actions to take, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: Give the scheduled tramadol dose for back pain
Encourage oral fluids and reassess in 4 hours
Hold the next sertraline and tramadol doses
Give oral diphenhydramine for the agitation
Notify the provider of suspected serotonin toxicity

exhibit.title: Nurses' Notes, 1530
exhibit.text: Client, 58 years old, takes sertraline 150 mg PO daily for major depressive disorder. Tramadol 50 mg PO every 6 h started 2 days ago for back pain. Now restless and agitated, diaphoretic, with 3 loose stools since noon. Fine tremor of both hands; reflexes 3+ with inducible ankle clonus. Skin flushed and moist. T 38.6 °C, HR 122/min, BP 162/94 mm Hg, RR 22/min.

rationale.short: Sertraline plus tramadol, then mental-status change, autonomic instability and neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia): serotonin syndrome.

c3.text: Label lists agitation, tachycardia, labile BP, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, tremor, hyperreflexia and diarrhea.

c4.text: Needs an antipsychotic; rigidity rather than clonus.

c1.text: Skin would be dry and hot, not diaphoretic.

c2.text: He is taking an opioid, not stopping one.

a3.text: Label: discontinue the SSRI and concomitant serotonergic agents immediately.

a1.text: Tramadol is a listed serotonergic precipitant.

a4.text: Anticholinergic; does not treat the cause.

a2.text: Delays care of a potentially life-threatening reaction.

expanded.takeaway: Clonus + hyperreflexia + a new serotonergic drug = stop the serotonergic drugs and escalate.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: 1 point for each correct response; no deduction for incorrect responses.

items.stem: A client with a chronic endocrine disorder arrives after 2 days of vomiting. Complete the diagram: choose the condition the client is **most** likely experiencing, 2 actions to take, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL over the first hour
Wait for the cortisol result before giving a steroid
Give the usual oral hydrocortisone dose with an antiemetic
Restrict fluids to 1,000 mL per day

exhibit.title: Emergency Department, 0640
exhibit.text: Client, 34 years old, primary adrenal insufficiency, takes hydrocortisone 10 mg PO each morning and 5 mg each afternoon plus fludrocortisone. Vomiting for 2 days; has not kept any doses down. Diffuse abdominal pain, confused to time. BP 78/44 mm Hg, HR 128/min, T 37.9 °C. Na 126 mEq/L, K 5.8 mEq/L, glucose 62 mg/dL. Cortisol and ACTH drawn 0635; results pending.

rationale.short: Known adrenal insufficiency, missed doses, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia mean adrenal crisis. Treat immediately with parenteral hydrocortisone and isotonic saline.

c2.text: Classic crisis: hypotension, abdominal pain, Na down, K up, glucose down.

c4.text: Does not explain the hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia.

c1.text: Euvolemic with low Na, not shock.

a2.text: Endocrine Society: hydrocortisone 100 mg parenterally immediately.

a1.text: Isotonic saline 1,000 mL within the first hour.

a3.text: Never delay steroids for test results; samples are already drawn.

a4.text: Oral route fails with vomiting and shock.

m1.text: Electrolytes and hypoglycemia correct with treatment.

expanded.takeaway: Suspected adrenal crisis: give stress-dose hydrocortisone first. Labs can wait.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: 1 point for each correct response; no deduction for incorrect responses.

items.stem: A client receiving an IV antibiotic develops new symptoms. Complete the diagram: choose the condition the client is **most** likely experiencing, 2 actions to take, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: When restarted per prescriber, infuse over at least 150 minutes
Record a permanent vancomycin allergy and request a different antibiotic
When restarted per prescriber, infuse over 60 minutes
Give the remaining dose at the current rate after the itching settles

exhibit.title: Nurses' Notes, 1035
exhibit.text: Client, 46 years old, 80 kg. Vancomycin 1,500 mg in 300 mL 0.9% NaCl started 1020; pump found running at 600 mL/h. At 1035: intense itching and erythematous flushing of face, neck and upper chest. Speaking in full sentences; no wheeze or stridor; lips and tongue normal. BP 104/64 mm Hg (128/78 at 1015), HR 104/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Tolerated vancomycin on a previous admission.

rationale.short: Flushing and pruritus of the upper body with mild hypotension during a too-fast vancomycin infusion, with no airway signs and prior tolerance, is a rapid-infusion reaction.

c3.text: Label links rapid infusion to flushing, pruritus and hypotension.

c1.text: No airway, wheeze, or shock; prior tolerance.

a5.text: Label: stopping usually ends the reaction promptly.

a1.text: No faster than 10 mg/min and at least 60 min: 1,500 mg needs at least 150 min.

m2.text: Hypotension can progress with rapid infusion.

expanded.takeaway: Vancomycin time = the longer of 60 min or dose divided by 10 mg/min.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: 1 point for each correct response; no deduction for incorrect responses.

items.stem: A client in septic shock has a change at the IV site. Complete the diagram: choose the condition the client is **most** likely experiencing, 2 actions to take, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: Deep vein thrombosis of the arm
Stop the norepinephrine infusion at the infiltrated right forearm site, then promptly restart it through the left antecubital IV
Prepare phentolamine 5-10 mg in 10-15 mL 0.9% NaCl for infiltration of the area as prescribed
Flush the right forearm cannula with saline to clear the drug
Continue the infusion at the same site with hourly checks
Stop norepinephrine until a central line is placed
Color, temperature and capillary refill of the affected area

exhibit.title: ICU Flowsheet, 0215
exhibit.text: Client, 67 years old, septic shock. Norepinephrine 8 mcg/min infusing through a 20-gauge right forearm peripheral IV; central line placement scheduled for 0700. A second 18-gauge IV in the left antecubital vein has 0.9% NaCl at 30 mL/h. At 0215: skin over the right forearm IV is pale, cool and swollen along the vein; client reports burning. MAP 66 mm Hg.

rationale.short: Blanched, cool, swollen tissue along a norepinephrine IV is extravasation with vasoconstrictive ischemia. Stop the infusion at the infiltrated site, promptly restart the vasopressor through another vein, and treat the site with phentolamine.

c2.text: Blanching and cold skin reflect local vasoconstriction.

c3.text: Norepinephrine causes ischemia; not a simple infiltrate.

c4.text: Local blanching at the IV site.

a1.text: Stop flow into tissue; label: infuse into a large vein and avoid abrupt discontinuation, so restart promptly.

a2.text: Label dose; most effective within 12 h.

a5.text: Hours off pressor: abrupt cessation causes marked hypotension.

m4.text: Confirms perfusion during the line change.

expanded.takeaway: Vasopressor extravasation: stop at the bad site, restart promptly in a good vein, antidote the tissue.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: 1 point for each correct response; no deduction for incorrect responses.

items.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes is admitted with confusion. The unit's hyperglycemic crisis protocol follows the 2024 ADA/EASD consensus report. Complete the diagram: choose the condition the client is **most** likely experiencing, 2 actions to take, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: Give subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every 1-2 hours instead of an IV infusion
Infuse isotonic crystalloid at 500-1,000 mL/h initially
After initial fluid resuscitation, start a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/h
Begin with 0.45% sodium chloride because of hyperosmolality
Capillary glucose every 1-2 hours, aiming for a decline that does not exceed 90-120 mg/dL/h
Serum osmolality, aiming for a fall of no greater than 3.0-8.0 mOsm/kg/h

exhibit.title: Admission Data, 2210
exhibit.text: Client, 61 years old, 80 kg, type 2 diabetes (metformin), no heart or kidney disease history. Poor intake and urinary frequency for 5 days; confused today. Mucous membranes dry. BP 98/60 mm Hg, HR 116/min. Glucose 948 mg/dL, calculated serum osmolality 338 mOsm/kg, venous pH 7.35, bicarbonate 21 mEq/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.6 mmol/L, Na 132 mEq/L, K 4.4 mEq/L, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL.

rationale.short: Severe hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality without significant ketonemia or acidosis is HHS. Use isotonic fluids, low-dose insulin, and slow correction.

a3.text: 500-1,000 mL/h for 2-4 h; no cardiac or renal disease.

a4.text: After fluids; no significant ketosis or acidosis: 0.05 units/kg/h (4 units/h).

a1.text: Consensus: SC rapid-acting analogs are not recommended in HHS.

a5.text: Hypotonic fluid only if osmolality is not falling.

m1.text: Glucose every 1-2 h; decline >90-120 mg/dL/h risks cerebral edema.

m4.text: Ketones are not the problem; urine tests are unreliable.

expanded.takeaway: HHS: fluids first, half-dose insulin, and correct slowly.

exhibit.title: Client, 74 years old, hospitalized for aspiration pneumonia with poor oral intake. Phenytoin 100 mg IV every 8 h for a seizure disorder.
exhibit.text:
Laboratory Results and Assessments
| | Day 1 | Day 5 | Day 9 |
| Total phenytoin (10-20 mcg/mL) | 12 mcg/mL | 15 mcg/mL | 16 mcg/mL |
| Albumin (3.5-5.0 g/dL) | 3.6 g/dL | 2.6 g/dL | 2.0 g/dL |
| Creatinine (0.6-1.1 mg/dL) | 0.8 mg/dL | 0.8 mg/dL | 0.9 mg/dL |
| Assessment | Alert, steady gait | Mild dizziness | Horizontal nystagmus, unsteady wide-based gait, slurred speech, somnolent |

rationale.short: Dose-related neurotoxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech, somnolence) despite a 'therapeutic' total level. Albumin fell from 3.6 to 2.0, raising the free fraction.

d1.text: Label lists these as dose-related reactions. A stroke would be focal and sudden; signs of toxicity rule out subtherapeutic or expected.

d2.text: Label: with hypoalbuminemia, unbound concentration is more relevant. Trough timing and normal creatinine do not explain toxicity; a normal total level is the trap.

d3.text: Hold and escalate with a free level. Giving the dose continues toxicity; food does not apply to IV.

expanded.takeaway: Low albumin + phenytoin: trust the free level and the neuro exam, not the total level.

payload.template: The trend is most consistent with {{d1}}. The nurse should first {{d2}}. The nurse should also monitor {{d3}}.

exhibit.title: Client, 31 years old, acute psychosis, admitted to the inpatient psychiatric unit. Haloperidol started day 1; dose increased day 3. No other medications.
exhibit.text:
Flowsheet
| | Day 1 | Day 3 | Day 4 |
| Temperature | 37.0 °C | 38.1 °C | 39.6 °C |
| HR / BP | 80/min, 124/78 | 104/min, 148/96 | 128/min, 176/102 then 98/60 |
| Muscle tone | Normal | Stiff arms | Generalized rigidity; reflexes diminished |
| Mental status | Guarded | Withdrawn, slow to respond | Mute, confused, staring |
| CK (30-200 units/L) | 150 | 2,400 | 18,600 |
| Urine | Clear yellow | Clear yellow | Tea-colored, 20 mL/h |

rationale.short: Rising fever, rigidity, altered mental status and labile BP after a haloperidol increase, with CK 18,600 and tea-colored urine, is NMS with rhabdomyolysis.

d1.text: Label: NMS = hyperpyrexia, muscle rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, raised CK. Serotonin syndrome has clonus and hyperreflexia, not reduced reflexes. Dystonia has no fever or CK rise. Catatonia does not explain fever or CK.

d2.text: Label: immediately stop antipsychotics. More haloperidol worsens NMS; benztropine with continued drug is wrong; seclusion delays medical care.

d3.text: Myoglobinuria and acute renal failure can follow. Lithium, peak flow and lipids are unrelated.

expanded.takeaway: Fever + rigidity + high CK on an antipsychotic = NMS: stop the drug and treat it as a medical emergency.

exhibit.title: Client, 31 years old, G2P1 at 30 weeks, gestational diabetes diagnosed at 26 weeks. Medical nutrition therapy and walking after meals for 3 weeks. Glucose log reviewed at a prenatal visit.
exhibit.text:
Self-monitored glucose (mg/dL), weekly averages
| | Week 1 | Week 2 | Week 3 |
| Fasting | 99 | 101 | 104 |
| 1 h after breakfast | 136 | 132 | 129 |
| 1 h after lunch | 131 | 128 | 126 |
| 1 h after dinner | 138 | 134 | 133 |

rationale.short: Every fasting average is >=95 and rising, while all 1-hour postprandial values are below 140. Nutrition therapy is not meeting the fasting goal, so insulin is the preferred agent.

d1.text: Fasting 99-104 vs goal <95; 1-h values 126-138 vs goal <140.

d2.text: ADA 15.15/15.17: add insulin if goals are not met; it is preferred. Metformin and glyburide should not be first-line (15.21). Waiting 4 more weeks prolongs fetal exposure.

d3.text: ADA 15.8: fasting <95 mg/dL. 105, 120 and 70-130 are not pregnancy fasting goals.

expanded.takeaway: GDM targets: fasting <95; 1-h <140 or 2-h <120. If they are not met with lifestyle changes, start insulin.
